Essential revisions:

The reviews on this version of the manuscript were mixed, with some definite enthusiasm for the inclusion of the new midget cell data, but some remaining skepticism and questions about the presentation and generality of the current results. Several points need to be fully addressed for this manuscript to be accepted:

1) For the section on interpreting the GLM as a conductance-based model, and the biophysical motivation for the paper:

The model is set up to make some mathematical manipulations in order to remove the voltage dependence of the currents. That wasn't super clear on a first or second pass and should be made more accessible to the reader.

Other points to address for clarity and scholarship:a) There exists a common quasi-biophysical interpretation of the GLM, wherein the output of the linear stage is thought of as an approximation of the intracellular input or voltage. This interpretation requires (1) that E and I inputs are thought of as currents and sum linearly. Near threshold, this approximation might be decent for modeling spiking, as the voltage is ~constant. (2) the integration time of the neuron must be short enough that the response is mostly a function of the inputs, not on its own voltage history. With these constraints presumed satisfied, many previous studies over the years have assumed that the generating function of the GLM has a quasi-biophysical basis. Can this more standard derivation/interpretation be addressed in this manuscript? Does the explicit integration in the "biophysical" GLM detailed in this work (which addresses assumption 2 above) help in fitting neuronal spiking as compared to a standard GLM? No explicit comparisons are made in the manuscript, and should be added.

b) The derivations seem overly long to simply notice that ge(V-Ee) – gi(V-Ei) will have no voltage dependence if ge and gi cancel. This derivation might be difficult to follow for the broad readership of this journal and should be explained more clearly.

c) This should be reorganized so that it doesn't distract from subsequent results. It could be made more clear that the E = -I assumption is made only to connect this to the GLM-like model class, to motivate the model setup, and is relaxed in the subsequent CBEM inference scheme.

2) For the CBEM model setup, justification, and background:a) The GLM derivation is what is used to motivate the CBEM, and excitation and inhibition are rectified (Equation 10 compared with Equation 9). While the motivation for such rectification is that conductances must be non-negative, this seems somewhat misleading. In the retina, rectification of excitation and inhibition (where it exists) often comes from other sources, most notably non-linear synaptic release from bipolar cells (see Schwartz et al., 2012, Turner and Rieke, 2016, and Freeman, 2015), as well as the effect of amacrine cell processing, which often preserve or extend non-linear effects. While conductances cannot be negative (as the authors assert), the rectification in Equation 10 probably has other sources. This issue raises concerns about the motivation for the CBEM and should be addressed and clarified.

b) The model in its current form cannot capture any cell for which either excitation or inhibition is a non-monotonic function of contrast (i.e. any cell with ON-OFF excitation or ON-OFF inhibition). This applies to many other RGC types, and likely most visual neurons downstream in the brain. Please discuss this limitation more fully and argue for the generality of the model. How does this limit the general utility of this approach outside the retina? Can this model be used to infer a larger class of different contrast-response function shapes? That would certainly be impressive, but doesn't appear to be within the reach of the current model.

c) The advances of the CBEM over previous work on models with separate LN components for excitatory and inhibitory inputs needs to be more thoroughly reviewed, placing the CBEM in the context of this work and arguing for its particular advances.

d) Rectification of the inputs (Equation 10) is the basis of the LNLN cascade model used in many papers over the years, starting with the work of Shapley and Victor and Korenberg and Sakai (in 1970s and 80s). It has been explicitly incorporated in likelihood-based models of the retina and LGN in more recent years (Butts et al., 2011) and most recently in (Maheswaranathan et al., 2018). This includes models that explicitly model excitation and inhibition in the retina using nearly equivalent mathematical forms as used in the current manuscript.

The fact that previous models use spike trains to infer excitation and inhibition does seem to detract a bit from the novelty of the CBEM, if the manuscript does not demonstrate why the CBEM's particular form leads to better inference (certainly the validation with intracellular data here is key to drawing these conclusions and is understood as the main innovation in the paper). Answering the following questions would also provide more biological insight into the success of the CBEM: Is the CBEM's ability to match measured excitatory and inhibitory conductances a result of the integration of currents? The rectification of inputs? The difference between conductance and current?

e) What does the restriction that the conductances are non-noisy do to the CBEM in terms of the types of cellular computations it can and cannot reproduce? Are there particular biophysical effects (e.g. stim-dependent spiking noise) that will be missed via this constraint?

3) For a reader interested in applying the method, it will likely be important to get a better feeling for the applicability and interpretability of the data, in particular when no intracellular data are available for comparison.

a) Important questions are, for example, whether the method also works for non-white-noise stimuli and what may be limitations for the applicability of the method, or the interpretation of the obtained filters as corresponding to actual excitatory or inhibitory conductances. If no data are available, simulations and/or thoughtful discussion could help address these concerns.

b) As a specific example, Figure 10 shows that the inhibitory component can capture surround effects, at least for OFF parasol cells. But is it clear that this actually corresponds to inhibition received by the ganglion cell and not a representation of presynaptic inhibition that nonlinearly interacts with excitatory signals? (Presynaptic effects appear to form a major part of the surround in parasol cells, see, e.g., discussion in Turner, Schwartz and Rieke, 2018.)

c) The method currently uses an explicit model and parameters of the output nonlinearity that are obtained from intracellular data. For pure extracellular data, these parameters (or the shape of the nonlinearity) will not be known a priori. How does that affect the model fitting? Can the parameters of the output nonlinearity be included in the fitting procedure?

4) The results concerning contrast adaptation could be shortened or omitted. The CBEM does a bit better than a GLM, but really, both fail at contrast adaptation because one needs to model it explicitly, as has been done in many previous models, including papers cited in this manuscript from the Baccus group.

5) Existing approaches for inferring excitation and inhibition from spike trains are incorrectly labeled in the Introduction as LN modeling, and only briefly mentioned as alternative to the CBEM in the third paragraph of the discussion. This should be corrected, and the CBEM should be presented in this fuller context.

[Editors’ note: further revisions were suggested before acceptance.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Inferring synaptic inputs from spikes with a conductance-based neural encoding model" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Michael Frank (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

1) To clarify a bit first: The main model comparison that was sought after by the reviewers had the following aim: Explain how the inference of conductances here (i.e. the biophysical basis of the CBEM) is the key ingredient in successfully predicting the E/I values, as opposed to LNLN models, which have more general nonlinearities (as compared to the GLM's). The reviewers agree with you that the goal here is not to outperform other models per se, in terms of fitting performance or whatnot, but to add interpretable knowledge about the underlying biophysics. The prompt, then, from the reviewers is this: show more clearly and directly how the biophysical assumptions in the CBEM are crucial for getting this E/I estimation right, which allows for the proper interpretation of the model results; show that it's not just the fact that the CBEM (like LNLN models) has a more generalized form of nonlinearity built into it. Essentially, that one needs to model the biophysics in this more correct way to get the right interpretation out.

Here's the concern spelled out more explicitly:

If the CBEM is no better (at predicting the E/I inputs to a cell) than other LNLN models that simply have voltage-like, LN approximations of excitatory and inhibitory inputs, this means that the biophysics presented here is somewhat misleading (at least in the sense that it has to do with considering conductances), which is the current basis of the paper.

Additionally, any more-flexible LNLN models (with many subunits) -- now several in the literature – would actually outperform the CBEM because they can include multiple subunits, and model more general nonlinearities.

It is very possible that the more explicit model of the biophysics in the CBEM would do better and its particular structure is therefore an advance – but the manuscript does not show or address this directly.

There were certainly some things said about this in the response to reviewers, and more of that should be entered into the paper as well.

2) You had a question in the response to reviewers about references for the "quasi-biophysical interpretation of the GLM". The Gerstner references are certainly great here, but please also cite (and if appropriate, discuss) Pillow et al., 2004 and 2005 (where the output of the linear term is explicitly treated as a voltage) and perhaps one of the more recent papers comparing GLM fits to intracellular data.

3) Please add a few more lines to the Discussion section outlining why you expect this model to be of broad utility beyond the retina. Specifically: what sorts of heuristics can a future user of the method employ to decide if the model's assumptions are appropriate for their data? Here, just saying a bit more to justify the breadth of the expected applicability of the model would be sufficient.

results.result: The authors provide a novel biophysical interpretation of the Poisson GLM as a conductance-based model where excitatory and inhibitory conductances are driven by equal and opposite linear filters, resulting in constant total conductance. This interpretation establishes the GLM as a special case of the CBEM with perfectly balanced excitation and inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C7 present a mathematically derived theoretical result showing the equivalence between the GLM and a constrained conductance-based model. The derivation is presented with explicit equations (Equations 6-9) and follows logically from the requirement that membrane potential be an affine function of the stimulus. This is a theoretical contribution that does not require experimental validation.

results.result: An LN model with soft-rectifying nonlinearity accurately captures the relationship between stimuli and excitatory/inhibitory synaptic conductances in ON parasol RGCs, accounting for 79±4% and 63±3% of variance respectively. This validates the CBEM's assumption that conductances can be modeled as rectified-linear functions of filtered stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10 and C42-C43 provide quantitative validation of the LN conductance model using intracellular voltage clamp recordings from 6 ON parasol cells. The soft-rectifying nonlinearity closely matched measured conductances (Figure 2), and the model was validated on held-out test data. Claim C41 provides biological justification through citations showing bipolar cells are well-characterized by LN models.

results.result: The parametric soft-rectified linear function for mapping membrane potential to spike rate closely approximated non-parametric estimates from dynamic clamp recordings, validating the CBEM's output nonlinearity choice. This differs from prior GLM work that found exponential nonlinearities superior, possibly due to the CBEM's cascade of two nonlinearities.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 is supported by comparison of parametric and non-parametric estimates in Figure 3c using dynamic clamp data from 2 ON parasol cells. Claim C44 notes the difference from prior work with appropriate citation. Claim C45 offers a plausible explanation for the discrepancy. The validation is limited to 2 cells but the match between parametric and non-parametric estimates is visually compelling.

results.result: The CBEM fit to extracellular spike trains alone can predict excitatory and inhibitory synaptic conductances with correlations of r=0.73±0.01 and r=0.69±0.03 respectively in ON parasol RGCs, validated against intracellular voltage clamp measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C13-C14 present the core experimental validation of the CBEM's ability to infer conductances from spikes. The predictions were validated using intracellular recordings from 6 ON parasol cells with held-out test stimuli (Figures 4-5). The correlations are substantial though lower than the LN model fit directly to conductances (r=0.89 and r=0.82), which is expected given the CBEM only has access to spike data.

results.result: The CBEM predicted conductances show systematic timing discrepancies compared to measured conductances in ON parasol cells: excitation precedes inhibition by 12.6±1.0 ms in CBEM predictions versus nearly zero lag (0.0±2.4 ms) in measurements, and predicted excitation precedes measured excitation by 5.6±0.7 ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 identify systematic timing errors in CBEM predictions with statistical testing (p<0.0001 for exc-inh lag, p=0.0005 for excitation timing). These are honest assessments of model limitations. The discrepancies are small (5-13 ms) but statistically significant across all 6 cells, suggesting systematic rather than random errors.

results.result: The CBEM successfully captures positively correlated excitation and inhibition in ON-midget cells, predicting excitatory conductances with r=0.85±0.03 and the timing relationship where excitation precedes inhibition by 8.2±0.8 ms (measured: 10.1±0.52 ms, p=0.06). However, inhibitory predictions were weaker (r=0.33±0.06) due to complex nonlinear behavior from mixed ON/OFF inhibitory inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 and C46-C47 demonstrate the CBEM can discover positive exc-inh correlations despite GLM initialization with opposite tuning (5 ON-midget cells). Excitatory predictions are strong (C19) and timing is well-captured (C47, p=0.06). The weaker inhibitory predictions (C20) are explained by biological complexity (C46) supported by citation. This shows both model capability and honest assessment of limitations.

results.result: The CBEM outperforms the GLM at predicting spike responses to novel stimuli in all 9 RGCs tested, achieving 86% vs 77% PSTH variance explained and 0.34±0.11 bits/spike improvement in log-likelihood.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 and C49 provide quantitative comparisons showing consistent CBEM superiority across all 9 cells using both PSTH prediction (C22) and single-trial log-likelihood (C23) metrics. The improvements are modest but consistent, and the result is replicated across multiple datasets (full-field, multi-contrast, spatio-temporal stimuli).

results.result: GLM prediction errors are anti-correlated with CBEM inhibitory conductance magnitude (p<0.0001), suggesting the CBEM's inhibitory conductance improves predictions by reducing firing when the GLM over-predicts spike rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25 provide mechanistic insight into why CBEM outperforms GLM through analysis of prediction errors and their relationship to predicted conductances. The anti-correlation is statistically significant (p<0.0001) and the interpretation (C25) follows logically from the analysis. This helps explain the performance differences observed in C22-C23.

results.result: The CBEMexc (excitation-only model) shows that the GLM stimulus filter accounts only for excitatory input in parasol cells, and still outperforms the GLM (81% vs 77% PSTH variance, 0.14±0.10 bits/sp improvement) despite lacking inhibition, which is consistent with prior findings that inhibition weakly modulates parasol responses to full-field noise.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 are supported by comparison of GLM and CBEMexc filters (nearly identical, Figure 8e) and performance metrics. Claim C26 provides biological context through citation. The CBEMexc's intermediate performance (better than GLM, worse than full CBEM) helps dissect the sources of CBEM's improvements. The interpretation that GLM captures excitation is reasonable given filter similarity.

results.result: The CBEM maintains predictive performance across contrast levels more accurately than the GLM, losing only 0.16±0.2 bits/sp at 24% contrast compared to GLM's 0.36±0.41 bits/sp loss. This demonstrates the CBEM's ability to capture contrast-dependent gain changes through interactions between excitatory and inhibitory conductances.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 and C52 show the CBEM better generalizes across contrasts (8 RGCs, 24-96% contrast). Claims C29-C30 provide biological and theoretical context through citations. The quantitative comparison (C31-C32) shows consistent CBEM advantage, particularly at lower contrasts. Claim C52 provides mechanistic interpretation linking conductance interactions to gain control, supported by the multi-contrast data.

results.result: The CBEM predicts that excitation and inhibition are most anticorrelated at 22% contrast for ON cells and 34% contrast for OFF cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 presents a specific prediction from CBEM fits to multi-contrast data. However, this prediction is not validated against measured conductances at different contrasts. The claim represents a model prediction rather than an experimentally verified result. Without intracellular validation across contrasts, the accuracy of this prediction remains uncertain.

results.result: For spatio-temporal stimuli, the CBEM predicted PSTHs more accurately than the GLM (83% vs 79% R²) and single-trial responses with 0.07±0.04 bits/sp improvement across 27 parasol RGCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 extend the CBEM's superior performance to spatio-temporal stimuli (27 cells). The improvements are more modest than for full-field stimuli, consistent with the authors' interpretation that spatial structure is needed to differentiate the models. The large sample size (27 cells) strengthens confidence in the result.

results.result: Spatial correlations in the stimulus differentiate the CBEM's predictions from the GLM, with center-surround stimuli producing distinct excitation-inhibition cross-correlation patterns compared to uncorrelated spatio-temporal or full-field noise.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by simulations showing different exc-inh cross-correlations for spatially correlated vs uncorrelated stimuli (Figure 11). The center-surround stimulus produced a positive peak at positive lags, contrasting with the negative correlation for full-field and uncorrelated spatio-temporal noise. This provides mechanistic insight into when CBEM and GLM predictions diverge.

results.result: The CBEM belongs to an extended family of non-GLM neural encoding models but uniquely links model components fit to spikes alone to experimentally measured conductances, differing from previous cascade approaches by explicit biophysical framework and direct validation in individual cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 and C50 position the CBEM within the broader modeling literature. C37 correctly classifies the CBEM as non-GLM due to nonlinear stimulus dependence. C38 and C50 make claims about uniqueness that are supported by the validation experiments (Figures 4-6) and appropriate citations to prior work. The distinction from prior cascade models is substantiated.

results.result: The CBEM's linear-rectified conductance model does not capture non-monotonic portions of stimulus-conductance nonlinearities observed in the data, likely because amacrine cells receive inputs from both ON and OFF channels.
results.evaluation: Claim C39 honestly identifies a limitation of the CBEM visible in Figure 2c,e where the soft-rectifying nonlinearity fails to capture non-monotonic regions. The biological explanation is supported by appropriate citations. This represents good scientific practice in acknowledging model limitations with mechanistic explanation.

results.result: The CBEM models conductances and membrane potential as deterministic functions of the stimulus with all stochasticity confined to spike generation, which makes the likelihood tractable for efficient fitting while capturing key features like shunting inhibition and time-varying gain.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C51 describe the CBEM's computational tractability, while C54-C55 explain the deterministic modeling assumptions. These are accurate descriptions of the model structure supported by the mathematical formulation (Equations 10-17) and successful parameter estimation. The trade-off between biophysical realism and computational tractability is clearly stated.

results.result: The Poisson GLM has been widely applied across brain areas, but in retina and other sensory areas where excitatory and inhibitory inputs have substantially different tuning, a single linear filter is insufficient to describe stimulus integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 provide background context for the work. C4 is well-supported by multiple citations to GLM applications. C5 is supported by citations to experimental studies showing differential tuning. C6 follows logically from C5. These claims accurately represent prior work and motivate the need for the CBEM.

results.result: The reliability of RGC spike trains depends on the stochasticity of synaptic conductances, and noise correlations between excitatory and inhibitory conductances may affect encoding.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 is supported by appropriate citations to prior experimental work. This represents an honest acknowledgment of a limitation of the CBEM's deterministic conductance model and suggests directions for future work. The claim accurately represents prior findings.

results.result: The CBEM can help reveal circuit-level computations that support perception under naturalistic conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is a forward-looking statement about potential applications. While the CBEM's ability to infer conductances from spikes is demonstrated, the claim that this will help reveal circuit computations under naturalistic conditions is speculative. The spatio-temporal results (C34-C36) provide some support, but naturalistic stimuli were not tested.
